challenges.name: queue-lag-and-age-quiz
challenges.title: Depth, age and wait time on the grading queue
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the evening the grading queue looked normal on the depth panel while learners waited minutes for their results.

questions.question:
Grading queue dashboard, one row per sample (depth = jobs waiting, completed = jobs finished in the previous minute):

time   depth  completed/min  in_flight  oldest_age
17:40   240        420           8         0m 41s
18:40   238         38           6         6m 12s

Two of the eight grading workers were crash-looping from 18:05; and code runner calls on the other six took about 9 s instead of about 1 s.

Statement: "Depth is the same at both samples, yet a submission that joins the queue at 18:40 waits roughly six minutes, while at 17:40 it waited well under a minute."
questions.explanation: True. How long a new job waits depends on how many jobs are ahead of it and how fast they leave: about depth / throughput. At 17:40 that is 240 / 420 per minute, about 34 seconds; at 18:40 it is 238 / 38 per minute, about 6.3 minutes, which the oldest_age column confirms (6m 12s). Depth stayed flat because learners submitted less in the evening while workers drained much more slowly. The misconception this tests is that depth measures delay: depth is a count, and the same count can mean 30 seconds or 6 minutes depending on throughput. The age of the oldest waiting job measures the delay directly, which is why it is the number to put on the dashboard and the alert.

questions.question:
The worker records wait time when it takes a job:

worker.on("active", (job) => {
  waitSeconds.observe((Date.now() - job.timestamp) / 1000); // histogram, per queue
});

Grading panel, wait time p95 per minute:
18:48  4.1 s
18:49  3.8 s
18:50  (no data)
18:51  (no data)
18:52  (no data)
18:53  (no data)
18:54  (no data)
18:55  296 s

Deploy log: 18:50:02 all grading workers stopped (bad image), 18:55:10 rollback finished. Submissions kept arriving the whole time.

Statement: "Between 18:50 and 18:54 the wait-time panel shows no slow jobs, so learners who submitted in that period waited no more than a few seconds."
questions.explanation: False. Wait time is observed only when a worker takes a job. With every worker stopped, nothing was taken, so no samples were recorded and the panel shows no data, while every submission from 18:50 was waiting and getting older. The 296 s p95 at 18:55 is those jobs finally being taken after the rollback. A metric recorded at dequeue only describes jobs that have already left the queue: it is blind exactly when the queue is stuck. The misconception is reading "no data" or a low wait-time percentile as "healthy". Sample the age of the oldest waiting job on a timer (a gauge, or the broker's own metric such as SQS ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage) so a stuck queue shows a line that climbs one minute per minute.

challenges.name: queue-lag-report
challenges.title: Queue lag report from the worker event log
hints: For each metric, which one timestamp of a job do you need, and in which window does it count? If you first collapse every job to one record, does the order of the lines in the file still matter?

Look at three places: building one record per queue + jobId (keep the smallest timestamp of each type, and skip jobs without an enqueue at the end), the waiting test at the end of a window (a dequeue or a complete before end means the job is no longer waiting), and the rank of a percentile (ceil(p / 100 * n), counted from 1).

A similar case on the emails queue: job a enqueued 10:00:10, dequeued 10:00:40, completed 10:01:05; job b enqueued 10:00:30 and never dequeued. Window 10:00: a is in flight, so depth is 1 (b) and the oldest age is 10:01:00 - 10:00:30 = 30 s; a's wait of 30 s gives p50 = p95 = 30. Window 10:01: depth 1, oldest age 90 s, no waits (null), a's processing time of 25 s gives p95 = 25. For the waits [9, 1, 8, 3]: sorted [1, 3, 8, 9], p50 is rank ceil(2) = 2 -> 3 and p95 is rank ceil(3.8) = 4 -> 9.

tests.name: One grading queue over two minutes: depth, oldest age, wait and processing percentiles
Two queues sorted by name; a stuck email job breaches the 90 s SLO
Out-of-order and duplicated lines, plus a redelivery, give the clean report
In-flight jobs and a job whose dequeue line was lost are not waiting
Malformed lines are skipped and counted; a job with no enqueue is ignored
Nearest-rank p50/p95 over 20 waits, an empty minute, age exactly at the SLO
Large shuffled log: 3 queues, 540 jobs, 30 minutes, a stall in certificates
